Wednesday, midnight.
I don't know how to write this. At about eight, on the lane behind the market, a man stepped out and my car hit him. He fell. People started running towards the car, shouting. I was so scared of the crowd that I pressed the accelerator and drove away.
I drove around for an hour. My hands wouldn't stop. I kept seeing him on the ground.
At ten I called Jeevan and told him everything. He said, "You have to go back and tell the police. Now. Tell your father." I told Papa. He didn't shout. He just picked up the car keys and we went to the police station together.
At the station they said a shopkeeper had taken the man to hospital nearly twenty minutes after I left. He has a broken leg. The officer said leaving had made everything much worse, for him and for me.
I left a man lying in the road because I was afraid.

I took Papa's old waterproof trekking bag and packed it with Preeti's help. Aadhaar cards, ration card, property papers, all in two zip bags. A torch with spare batteries. I wrote the plan on a card and put it in the bag. Hung the bag by the door.
It's strange, but I feel calmer tonight than I did yesterday.

After last year's cyclone knocked out power and phones for a day and a half, I sat down in May and asked myself: what if it happens again, but for two days?
First problem: I don't know anyone's number by heart. So I wrote a paper list, with Mummy, Papa, my uncle in Vizag, our neighbour Pankaj bhaiya, the local police station and the hospital, and put it in a zip bag.
Second: no internet means no maps. I downloaded an offline map of the city and bought a small battery radio for news.
Third: who calls whom? I made a simple chain with the family: if we're separated, everyone tries Papa first. If Papa can't be reached, we try my uncle outside the city, since outside lines might work when ours don't.
We tested it in August. It worked. I'm Tarun, and planning for silence turned out to be half the preparation.

subtype: Approach: rumours and forwarded messages shape decisions [Pitfall]
passage:
In their small town below the dam, Indu's phone buzzed nonstop at nine at night. A voice message, forwarded many times: "Dam has burst! Water coming in one hour! Run!"
Her heart hammered. She forwarded it to three family groups before she'd even finished listening. Within minutes, people were out on the main road on scooters and tractors, heading for the highway. The road had been closed at the bridge because of landslides, and soon nothing could move.
Her friend Uday called. "Did you check it? The district collector's page says the dam is safe. They're only releasing water slowly, and the town is not being evacuated."
Indu opened the page. He was right. The weather department said the same.
She deleted her forwards, then wrote in each group: "The dam message is false. Please check the district collector's page before sharing." Her aunt replied, "Thank you, we were about to leave."

qa.q: What did the district collector's page say about the dam?
qa.a: It said the dam was safe and water was only being released slowly, with no evacuation.

qa.q: How did Indu feel when the voice message arrived?
qa.a: She felt panicked, heart hammering, and forwarded it to three groups before even finishing listening.

qa.q: What should Indu do next time a frightening message arrives?
qa.a: Check the district collector's page or weather department first, before forwarding anything, so a false alarm doesn't spread.

qa.q: How was Indu's aunt affected by the correction?
qa.a: Her aunt was relieved and grateful, saying they were about to leave onto the blocked roads.

grounding: Shows a forwarded rumour about a dam burst causing people to rush onto blocked roads, and the student checking official channels and stopping sharing.

subtype: Approach: rumours and forwarded messages shape decisions [Pitfall]
passage:
The message hit every group chat in the Austrian valley town at once: "The upper dam has cracked. Evacuate NOW." Oskar's phone showed it five times in two minutes.
Downstairs, his neighbours were already loading cars. The main road out was jammed within ten minutes. An ambulance trying to reach the old people's home was stuck behind them.
Oskar was about to forward it to his football team when Valentina, his flatmate, grabbed his wrist. "Wait. Where's it from?"
Neither knew. Valentina opened the regional emergency service's website. The top notice read: "Reports of a dam failure are false. Dam is under normal monitoring. Please keep roads clear."
Oskar deleted his half-typed forward and posted the official link in the team chat instead, with one line: "Checked. It's false." Two teammates replied that they'd turned back. The ambulance, eventually, got through.

qa.q: What did the regional emergency service's notice say?
qa.a: It said reports of a dam failure were false and asked people to keep roads clear.

qa.q: How was Oskar feeling when he nearly forwarded the message?
qa.a: He was alarmed and rushed, getting the message five times in two minutes and about to pass it on without checking.

qa.q: What else could Oskar do to help limit panic in future?
qa.a: He could save the regional emergency service's site on his phone and share it with the team in advance, so everyone checks there first.

qa.q: How might the ambulance crew have felt stuck on the jammed road?
qa.a: The crew were likely frustrated and worried, unable to reach the old people's home because of a false alarm.

grounding: Shows a forwarded dam rumour sending people onto jammed roads, and the student checking official channels and stopping the spread.
